tour.title: Rattanakosin: Grand Palace, Wat Pho & Wat Arun
tour.summary: The royal island where Bangkok began — the Grand Palace and the Emerald Buddha, the Reclining Buddha of Wat Pho, and a commuter ferry across the Chao Phraya to Wat Arun for sunset.
tour.overviewText:
Bangkok was a village with a customs post until a king with a broken kingdom decided to build a capital from scratch. In 1767 Burmese armies burned Ayutthaya, the old Siamese capital, to the ground. Fifteen years of chaos later, a general who had fought his way back from Cambodia took the throne as Rama I, moved the seat of power across the Chao Phraya River, and in 1782 began a new city on a bend in the water. He dug canals along the eastern side to turn the site into an island — Rattanakosin, the historic core of today's Bangkok — and in the same year raised a palace, a royal chapel and a city pillar. Almost everything on this walk is the founding act of modern Thailand.

The Chao Phraya is the key to all of it. For two centuries it was the city's highway: no roads worth the name, so rice, teak, soldiers, monks and kings all moved by boat. Bangkok grew outward from this riverbank, and the boats still run — commuter ferries cross every few minutes, express boats hammer up and down, and the city's older, slower life is visible from the water. The river is also why the temples face the way they do, and why the palace stands with its back to the water and its gates to the land.

The faith you will meet here is Theravada Buddhism — the oldest surviving school of Buddhism, which reached Southeast Asia from Sri Lanka — and it is not a museum religion. Thai men commonly ordain as monks for a period, laypeople make merit by feeding monks at dawn, and temple compounds double as schools and community centres. The kings of the Chakri dynasty, the line that has ruled since 1782, are formally the protectors of that faith, which is why a royal chapel holds the country's most sacred Buddha image and why monarchy and Buddhism are hard to prise apart. Alongside the Buddhism sits an older layer of Brahmanical ceremony and spirit belief — the city pillar, the ploughing ritual on the royal field — and Thai religion is the blend of all of it. Expect to take your shoes off, keep shoulders and knees covered, never point your feet at a Buddha, and treat working monks as people going about their day rather than exhibits.

The walk itself is short and flat — about three kilometres, mostly level pavement — but it is not a stroll. It begins among the royal monuments and temple halls of the old city, drops through a two-hundred-year-old riverside market, and ends across the water as the sun goes down. You cross the Chao Phraya on the little public ferry from Tha Tien, the same crossing Bangkok commuters use every day.

Come early. Mid-May is the tail of the hot season — mid-thirties and humid — and the palace is both shadeless and mobbed after ten, so be at the gate for opening, carry water, and save the open-air sights for the cooler ends of the day. Palace, temple and prang tickets are separate and prices move; check at each gate. The reward is the last half-hour: Wat Arun's spire turning gold over the river as the city lights come on.
tour.difficulty: Easy, flat walking — about three kilometres of level pavement — but hot, humid and crowded, with long periods on your feet. Not strenuous in distance; demanding in heat and standing. Wat Arun's prang stairs are very steep and narrow.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at the Grand Palace gate for the 08:30 opening to beat the heat and the tour buses. Work north to Sanam Luang and the City Pillar Shrine, then south to Wat Pho and the river, and time the ferry to Wat Arun for the last hour before sunset, when the spire turns gold and then lights up. Mid-May is hot and humid — carry water and expect mid-thirties.

stops.name: Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew
stops.narration:
Be at the gate for opening — half past eight — because this is the one sight in the city that genuinely punishes lateness. By ten the tour buses are here, the courtyards are shadeless, and the queue for the Emerald Buddha snakes the length of a football pitch. The ticket is 500 baht, sold until half past three; verify at the gate, and note that it also buys you entry to the Dusit Palace museums for seven days. Before you go in: shoulders and knees covered, no see-through clothing. Sarongs are lent at the entrance.

This is the Grand Palace, Phra Borom Maha Ratcha Wang, and it has been the official residence of Thailand's kings since 1782. That year a general named Chao Phraya Chakri took the throne after the fall of the previous dynasty, reigned as Rama I, moved the capital across the river from Thonburi, and started building here. He was short of money, so the first palace was timber; the bricks came later, many of them carted downstream from the ruins of Ayutthaya, the old capital the Burmese had burned in 1767. The Chinese merchants who lived on this spot were moved south to what is now Chinatown. The compound covers about 218,000 square metres, and only part of it is open: the king still uses the rest for ceremonies.

The temple inside the walls, Wat Phra Kaew, is not really a temple — no monks live here. It is a royal chapel, built to hold one object: the Emerald Buddha. Look at it and the first surprise is the size. It is about 66 centimetres tall, carved from a green stone usually described as jade but probably jasper, and dressed in gold. The second surprise is the story. It surfaced in Chiang Rai in 1434, so the legend goes, when lightning struck a stupa and the plaster flaked off a hidden image. It travelled through northern Thailand and Laos, was carried off to Vientiane, and in 1779 was brought back to Siam as war booty. It stood briefly at Wat Arun across the river, then was installed here in 1785, when this chapel was finished. The Thai state treats it as its palladium — the talisman whose possession legitimises the ruler — and the king changes its golden costume three times a year to mark the hot, rainy and cool seasons.

Walk the cloister that rings the chapel, because its inner wall carries one continuous painted epic: the Ramakien. That is Thailand's version of the Ramayana, the ancient Indian tale of the prince Rama, his abducted wife Sita, the monkey warrior Hanuman, and the ten-headed demon king Thotsakan — Ravana in the Indian original. The panels were first painted under Rama I and repainted several times since, which is why they look so fresh; treat them as a living tradition, not a fixed mural.

And look up at the gates. The giant figures guarding them are yaksha — demons from the Ramakien, several metres tall, in green, white and gold. The most famous is Thotsakan himself, the green giant; his counterpart on another gate is Sahatsadecha, the white one. They are meant to look terrifying, and they do.

Two more things before you leave. Near the chapel stands a scale model of Angkor Wat, the vast temple in Cambodia — a reminder that Siam's kings measured themselves against the Khmer empire they had absorbed. And the building with the European columns and the Thai roof is the Chakri Maha Prasat, built in 1876: Rama V wanted a Western palace, his court insisted on a Siamese crown, and the compromise is one of the strangest, most confident buildings in the city. Inside the chapel, no photographs and no shoes; sit with your feet pointing away from the Buddha. When you have had enough, leave by the north gate onto Na Phra Lan Road.
stops.entranceFeeNote: 500 ฿ for foreign visitors; the ticket includes entry to the Dusit Palace museums for seven days, and the audio guide is extra. Prices and rules change — verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Daily 08:30–16:30; tickets sold until 15:30. Occasionally closed or partly closed for royal ceremonies — check before you go.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level paved courtyards, but a lot of standing, little shade and heavy crowds. Some halls have steps. The heat is the real obstacle rather than the ground.
stops.insiderTip: Be at the gate for the 08:30 opening and go straight to the Emerald Buddha chapel before the tour groups arrive, then do the Ramakien cloister and the palace halls at leisure. The ticket includes the Dusit Palace museums for a week — keep it.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the palace by the north gate onto Na Phra Lan Road. Cross the road and walk about eight hundred metres north into the open field — that is Sanam Luang. Head for the tamarind trees around the middle.

stops.name: Sanam Luang (Royal Field)
stops.narration:
Cross the road and the city opens into a great bare field. This is Sanam Luang, the royal ground — about 119,000 square metres of it, with a double ring of tamarind trees around the edge and not much in the middle. It has been here since 1784, and for most of its life it had a more solemn job than it does now. Its original name was Thung Phra Men, the royal cremation ground, and that is exactly what it was: the kings, queens and senior princes of the Chakri dynasty were burned here on enormous temporary pavilions, and the ashes gathered up. When King Bhumibol died in 2016, the crematorium raised on this field took months to build and drew hundreds of thousands of mourners. The scale is the point. In a Buddhist kingdom, the funeral of a king is a state event, and the state needed a stage this big.

It is not only a place of death. Every May, usually, the Royal Ploughing Ceremony is held here: oxen are yoked to a plough and offered a choice of foods, and the one they eat is read as a forecast for the rice harvest. The ritual is Brahmanical, not Buddhist — a reminder that Thai religion is a blend, with Hindu-Brahmin ceremony and older spirit beliefs layered under and alongside the Buddhism most people practise. Rama IV formalised it in the 1850s; the king still presides.

The field has a political history too, and it is worth knowing, because this square is where Thailand's two ideas of itself have collided. In October 1976, a student protest at neighbouring Thammasat University was broken up by police and right-wing militia in a massacre that left dozens dead; the students had gathered around this area. More recently, in 2020, pro-democracy protesters installed a plaque here calling for reform of the monarchy — it was removed within a day and the organisers charged with damaging a historical site. Supporters of the palace call the field a national symbol; critics point to the same ground as a place where dissent has been crushed. Both things are true, and the stones do not take sides.

Today it is simply the city's front lawn. At dawn it fills with joggers and with people feeding pigeons; by day it is mostly tourists walking between the palace and the temples; in the evening families spread mats and let children run. It is free and open, roughly five in the morning until ten at night. Rama V planted the first tamarind trees after a visit to Java in 1897, impressed by the gardens there; a second ring went in around 1967, and the trees now number in the hundreds. Look at the buildings on the far side: the Ministry of Defence with its cannons, and, at the southeastern corner, a small ornate shrine. That shrine is our next stop.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public field, open to all. It is a ceremonial and public space, not a ticketed site.
stops.accessibility: Flat open field, step-free throughout, with benches and shade at the tree-lined edges.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the cannons in front of the Ministry of Defence on the west side, and the tamarind ring — the first trees were planted by Rama V after a trip to Java. Early morning, when the field is full of joggers and pigeons, is its most local mood.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the field, walk to its southeastern corner, where the ornate pavilion with the spire stands near the Ministry of Defence — about five hundred metres. That is the City Pillar Shrine.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Adbar, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: City Pillar Shrine (San Lak Mueang)
stops.narration:
This small pavilion, and the two posts standing inside it, are the reason there is a Bangkok at all. The city pillar — san lak mueang, the shrine of the lak mueang, or 'city pillar' — was erected on 21 April 1782, months before the palace was finished, and it was the first building of the new capital. A city pillar is a post of chaiyaphruek wood, a kind of acacia whose name means 'tree of victory', buried upright so it stands as the axis of the settlement, with a horoscope for the city sealed inside. It is not a Buddhist object in origin. It belongs to the Brahmanical and animist layer of Thai religion: the pillar is the seat of Chao Pho Lak Mueang, the city's guardian spirit, and it was installed by Brahmin priests using astrological calculations. The same Brahmin tradition still runs the ploughing ceremony you passed on the field, and parts of the coronation. Thai Buddhism is not a single tidy thing; it is Theravada practice resting on a deep bed of spirits, guardians and ritual specialists.

The pillar you see first is not the original. Rama IV, King Mongkut, dug up the 1782 post in the 1850s, found it had rotted, and had a new, taller one — about five metres — made and installed in 1852; the old post was kept alongside it. Both were then housed in the pavilion with the spire you are looking at, modelled on the city-pillar shrine of Ayutthaya, the old capital. So the shrine holds two centuries of the same idea in one room.

There is a dark legend attached to the founding, and Thais tell it as a story rather than a fact: that the builders called out the words 'in, chan, mun, kong' in the four directions of the city, seized whoever answered, and buried them at the corners as guardian spirits. It appears in folklore, not in the royal chronicles, and the official accounts do not mention it — treat it as the kind of grim tale that grows around any foundation. What is documented is the traffic. People come here to pray for work, promotion, luck and health, because the guardian of a city is thought to be able to grant exactly those things. The standard offering is three incense sticks, a candle, a square of gold leaf, lotus flowers and a garland.

Entry is free. Hours are typically from early morning to early evening — around six to six, though they shift with ceremonies, so check at the gate. It is a sacred place rather than a tourist site: dress with shoulders and knees covered, and take your shoes off before the inner shrine. Then walk back out to the road and turn south; the long white wall on your left is the palace, and Wat Pho is about a kilometre down Sanam Chai Road.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry. It is a working shrine, not a ticketed site. Offerings are sold at the stalls by the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically daily, roughly 06:00–18:00; hours shift with ceremonies, so confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Level approach and a step or two into the shrine; shoes are removed before the inner shrine.
stops.insiderTip: Offerings are sold at the stalls by the gate — three incense sticks, a candle, gold leaf and a garland is the standard set. Watch how locals do it before joining in; this is a working shrine, not a photo stop.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the shrine, walk south down Sanam Chai Road for about a kilometre, keeping the long white palace wall on your right. Wat Pho's entrance, guarded by huge stone figures, is on the left at Thai Wang Road.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Suicasmo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Wat Pho (Reclining Buddha)
stops.narration:
Wat Pho is older than the city it stands in. There was a temple on this site in the Ayutthaya period, perhaps two centuries before Bangkok existed; Rama I rebuilt it from 1788, and his grandson Rama III enlarged it between 1832 and 1848 into the complex you are walking through. The name is a contraction of Wat Photaram — the monastery of the Bodhi tree, the fig tree at Bodh Gaya in India under which the Buddha is said to have found enlightenment. Locals call it Wat Phra Chetuphon, its formal name, but the old shorthand stuck.

The ticket is 300 baht, open from eight in the morning until half past seven; verify at the gate, since prices move. Cover your shoulders and knees, and remove your shoes before the halls. Brace for the crowd at the famous thing first, then slow down, because Wat Pho is a whole village of a temple: four great chedis, dozens of smaller ones, cloisters lined with hundreds of Buddha images, courtyards, gardens, and a working monastery on the far side of Chetuphon Road.

The Reclining Buddha is 46 metres long and 15 metres high, built under Rama III around 1832, with a brick core, plastered and gilded. It shows the Buddha at the moment of parinirvana — the passing into nirvana, the end of the cycle of rebirth, which is what 'reclining' means in Buddhist art; he is not sleeping. Walk the length of it and look at the feet: three metres high, inlaid with mother-of-pearl in 108 panels of auspicious symbols. One hundred and eight is a sacred number in Buddhism. Along the corridor behind the image is a row of 108 bronze bowls; you buy a cup of small coins and drop one into each bowl as you pass, a small act of merit that also helps pay for the temple.

Now the part most visitors miss. Rama III turned Wat Pho into a place of public learning — arguably Thailand's first university — by having diagrams and texts on medicine, massage, astrology, literature and history carved onto stone slabs and set into the walls and pavilions, so that anyone could come and read them. Those inscriptions were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2008. Look for the marble plaques showing figures with lines and pressure points on the body: those are the charts of traditional Thai massage.

Which brings us to the other thing Wat Pho is famous for. Traditional Thai massage — nuad Thai — was taught and practised here, and the temple runs a massage school and an on-site massage service; a thirty-minute session is around 340 baht, an hour around 520, and you should book ahead, because it is popular and the queues are real. Verify the prices when you arrive. Nuad Thai is not the oil massage you may be imagining: it is acupressure, rhythmic compression along the body's lines, and assisted stretching, closer to a guided yoga session than to a spa treatment, and it grew out of the medical knowledge inscribed on these very walls.

One more detail on the way out. The huge stone figures standing guard at the gates, some of them wearing wide hats and looking distinctly European, came to Siam as ballast in the holds of Chinese trading ships — heavy stone loaded low to steady a ship, then dumped on arrival. Thais put them to work as guardians. Remember that, because it is also the secret of a stop further along.
stops.entranceFeeNote: 300 ฿ for foreign visitors; free for children under 120 cm. The massage service is a separate fee (about 340/520/1,040 ฿ for 30/60/120 minutes). Verify at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Level courtyards with some steps into the halls; the Reclining Buddha hall has a short flight of steps. Good shade and benches along the way.
stops.insiderTip: Enter by the south gate on Chetuphon Road rather than the busy north one and you skip most of the crowd. The massage school at the back is the real thing — book a slot early in the day.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Wat Pho by the south gate onto Chetuphon Road, turn right and follow the lane west toward the river for about a hundred and fifty metres, until you reach the riverfront market and pier. That is Tha Tien.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tha Tien Pier & Market
stops.narration:
You have walked out of the temple and down to the river, into a small community that has been here for two hundred years. Tha Tien means, by one explanation, 'the flat pier', from a fire that levelled the area; by another, it comes from Ha Tien, a port in what is now southern Vietnam, because Vietnamese immigrants settled around here. Nobody is certain. What is certain is that this was the back door of the Grand Palace. The kings' consorts and their attendants used a small gate behind the palace to slip out and shop at the market here, which was famous for flowers, embroidery and handmade goods — one of the first land-based markets in Bangkok. Later it became a wholesale hub, especially for dried seafood, and in the reign of Rama V a Western-style theatre, the Prince Theatre, stood nearby. The market went quiet in the twentieth century when its trade was merged into Pak Khlong Talat, the big flower market to the south, and only recently has the area been tidied up for visitors.

But you are standing at a pier, and the pier is the point. Look at the river. The Chao Phraya is the reason Bangkok is here. Before there were roads worth the name, this was the city's highway: rice, teak, soldiers, monks, royal barges and ordinary passengers all moved by water, and the canals that laced the city were its side streets. Even now the river is a working artery, not a scenic backdrop. Count the traffic: long orange-flag commuter boats hammering up and down, long-tail taxis cutting across, and the little cross-river ferries shuttling people from bank to bank. More than fifteen boat lines run on the city's rivers and canals, and this pier — Tha Tien, N8 on the express-boat line — is one of the busiest.

The crossing you are about to make is the real thing, not a tourist ride. The ferry from Tha Tien to Wat Arun runs every few minutes, takes about two or three minutes to cross, and costs a few baht — around five at the time of writing, paid at the pier or on board, so carry small notes and verify the fare on the day. The people beside you are mostly commuters: students heading to universities on the far bank, office workers, monks. This is a public boat, not a cruise, and that is exactly why it is worth taking. Board it, stand where you can see, and watch the temple you are heading for grow out of the far bank.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The pier and market are free to walk. The cross-river ferry to Wat Arun costs a few baht — around 5 ฿; verify the fare and the last-boat time on the day.
stops.openingHours: The market is busy through the day. Cross-river ferries run frequently from early morning to early evening; confirm the last crossing on the day.
stops.accessibility: Flat riverfront and pier. Boarding the ferry involves a step down onto a moving deck; staff usually help.
stops.insiderTip: Stand on the upstream side of the pier for the best view of Wat Arun across the water. Carry small notes for the ferry — change is not always available.
stops.nextStopDirections: Board the cross-river ferry from Tha Tien to Wat Arun: it runs every few minutes, takes two or three minutes, and costs a few baht — around five, paid at the pier or on board. Verify the fare and the last-boat time on the day. You land at the Wat Arun pier; the prang is straight ahead.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Christophe95, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Wat Arun (Temple of Dawn)
stops.narration:
Wat Arun — the Temple of Dawn — takes its name from Aruna, the charioteer of Surya, the sun god in Hindu mythology: a strange name for a temple best seen at sunset, where this walk ends. The temple is older than Bangkok. It stood here in the Ayutthaya period, called Wat Makok after the hog-plum trees around it, later Wat Chaeng. Before Rama I moved the Emerald Buddha across the river in 1785, this is where it was kept. So the far bank, not the near one, was the sacred side first.

The tower in front of you is a prang — the tall, corn-cob-shaped spire that is the Khmer form of the stupa, a style Siam borrowed from the empire it admired and fought. This one was begun under Rama II and finished under Rama III in 1851; it stands between roughly 67 and 86 metres, depending on whose measurement you trust. The prang is Mount Meru, the mountain at the centre of the Hindu and Buddhist universe, with four smaller prangs around it for the surrounding continents and figures of gods and demons supporting the tiers. At the very top sits a seven-pronged trident, the weapon of the Hindu god Shiva.

Now look at the surface: here is the detail that changes how you see the whole building. The prang is not painted or tiled in the ordinary way. It is encrusted with broken Chinese porcelain — plates, bowls and cups, smashed and set into the plaster to form flowers, demons, elephants and geometric patterns — mixed with the shells of a large sea snail. That porcelain arrived as ballast. Chinese trading ships loaded heavy ceramics low in the hold to keep steady, then dumped them here, and Thai builders turned the broken crockery into ornament. The same trade, you will remember, delivered the stone giants to Wat Pho's gates. This is a temple decorated with the rubbish of international commerce, and it has outlasted the ships.

Around the base are the guardians: yaksha, demons from the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana. At the ordination hall stand two of the largest — Thotsakan, the green king of the demons, and Sahatsadecha, the white one — the same characters whose painted story covers the cloister at Wat Pho. The monkeys and demons holding up the prang's terraces are carved, not painted.

Climb as far as the stairs allow; the upper flight is very steep and narrow, and by midday the stone is too hot to touch, so use the handrail and take it slowly. From the terrace the geography clicks: Wat Pho's roofs to the south, the Grand Palace's gold and coloured tile to the north, and the river threading between them — the same water that carried the bricks from Ayutthaya and the porcelain from China. A big restoration between 2013 and 2017 replaced broken tiles and refaced the surfaces in lime plaster; some critics thought the result too clean and white, while the Fine Arts Department called it a return to the original look.

Entry is 200 baht for foreign visitors — verify at the gate, prices change — and the grounds are typically open 08:00–18:00. Shoulders and knees covered, shoes off in the ordination hall.

Stay for the light. The last half-hour before sunset is the reason to time the day this way: the porcelain catches the low sun and the spire turns from grey to gold, then the floodlights come on and it glows against the dark. When you are ready, take the ferry back to Tha Tien, or walk on into Thonburi for dinner on the quiet side of the river. You began at the founding shrine of a city that did not exist, crossed the palace and temple of the dynasty that made it, and end watching that city light up from the other bank. That is Rattanakosin in a day.
stops.entranceFeeNote: 200 ฿ for foreign visitors; verify at the gate, prices change.
stops.accessibility: Level temple grounds, but the prang stairs are very steep, narrow and uneven — not for anyone unsteady on their feet. The riverside terrace is level.
stops.insiderTip: Come an hour before sunset, climb the prang first while the light is still bright, then take the riverside terrace for the golden hour and the floodlights. The temple is usually far quieter late in the day than at midday.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Stay on the riverside terrace as the light goes: the prang turns gold, then the floodlights come on and it glows against the dark river. When you are ready, take the ferry back to Tha Tien — boats run until early evening, so confirm the last crossing — or walk on into Thonburi for dinner on the quieter side of the water.
